headline: Private credit remains a structurally attractive asset class for Australian investors but faces growing regulatory scrutiny on valuation practices and transparency
reasoning: Peter Szekely argues private credit continues to attract inflows due to its senior secured position in the capital structure, lower volatility than equity, and cash income characteristics. He notes it is relatively insulated from expensive equity and property valuations. However, he flags that ASIC has identified a wide disparity in valuation methodologies, related-party management, and fee treatment across managers, and is pushing for greater disclosure and transparency so investors truly understand what risk they are taking.
quote: I think the product is going to be with us, but sort of a focus in terms of giving investors something that's more investable... Private credit itself, you know, you'll remember it's a senior secured part of the capital structure ahead of equity. So any any issues with a borrower or credit issues are worn by equity first. So it has less volatility. It is a cash income product... given expensive equity markets, you know, relatively expensive property markets, it really, you know, remains an asset class that will continue to continue to attract inflows and should be, you know, a portion of investors portfolio holdings.
episode_title: The question private credit investors need to ask

headline: Valuation methodology disparities in Australian private credit create risk of unfair investor treatment, particularly in property-related funds
reasoning: Szekely explains there are two broad valuation approaches in the market. The first, which Tanarra employs, involves forward-looking probability-weighted default and loss assessments that feed into provisions. The second — more common in the market — values loans at par so long as no default has occurred and asset coverage exists. He warns this latter approach is especially problematic in multi-fund asset management groups where investments can be shifted between credit and private equity funds, allowing losses to be obscured and one investor class to be treated unfairly relative to another.
quote: Within the guidelines, there's sort of a wide range of methodologies you can use for establishing the valuations of the underlying loans on one end... you're going to look forward and on a name by name... what's the probability of potential default in the future, if that happens, what's the what would be the loss in that loan? And let's probably wait that back to today and potentially manage that through provisions in the portfolio. The other approach, which has been often typical in this market, has been let's look at the portfolio at this point of time today, all those no defaults... Let's just leave it at par. Um, and when that becomes an issue is, you know, especially for larger asset management groups, they might have 2 or 3 credit funds that might have a private equity fund... if you ever have the shift of investments from one fund to the other, from credit to private equity, for example, the valuation is critical because if you don't manage it fairly, one investor group is not being treated fairly.
episode_title: The question private credit investors need to ask

headline: APRA expects Australian default rates to rise as economic softness weighs on both private credit and banking sectors
reasoning: Szekely notes that APRA has flagged an expectation of rising defaults, consistent with economic data showing GDP growth of only 0.3% quarter-on-quarter versus 0.8% the prior quarter and inflation still elevated at 4%, well above the RBA target. He sees private credit and banking as interconnected given insurers and banks invest in private credit funds and banks also provide credit facilities to private credit managers. Despite these concerns, he notes private credit remains relatively small in Australia, limiting systemic risk to the banking sector.
quote: APRA has highlighted that they do expect defaults to increase. And again, that's reflected by the softest and the economies that we've seen. You know, first quarter GDP I think it was 0.3% quarter on quarter versus 0.8 in the end of last year. Um, inflation is still fairly elevated. You know, it's come down to 4% but still well above the RBA target rate. So I think there is concerns around softness. And the economy will end up into a pickup in defaults. And that's both private credit but also the banking sector... the positive is that private credit does remain fairly small in this market. Um, so there's no real concern among the regulator, including APA, that, you know, there will really be any material damage to the banking sector.

headline: Emphasises layered downside protection in private credit via senior positioning, covenants, and equity buffers as the asset class grows in popularity

headline: Tanarra Capital urges Lendlease to pursue demerger, exit international construction and reset strategy to unlock securityholder value
